# Platform wants one scheduling policy signed off for all three workloads

## Problem Description

On 1 September the platform team drained a node pool for a patch upgrade between
01:40 and 02:05 UTC. The monthly `close-books` run never happened. No alert, no
failed Job object, nothing in the dashboard - the controller simply did not
create the Job, and we found out on the 10th when Accounting asked where the
August close was. The manifests have not been touched since March.

Out of that, platform has drafted one scheduling standard to apply to every
CronJob in the cluster. It is in `ops/proposed-policy.md` and they want it signed
off so they can raise a single PR against all three manifests. The reasoning in
it is not silly and the person who wrote it has been carrying this incident for a
fortnight.

I am not signing something off because it reads as safer than what we have now.
Go through the draft properly, decide what you would actually apply and to which
workload, and change only what you can defend to the team that owns the job.

The three objects as they are in the cluster are in `k8s/`, platform's model of
the controller is `src/controller.js` and it has a test file that passes, the
cluster's own notes are in `ops/cluster.md` - including the requirement each
owning team gave us, which is the closest thing we have to a spec - and the two
incident write-ups are in `ops/` as well.

## Output Specification

1. Edit the objects under `k8s/` to whatever you sign off on, and leave every
   field you are not acting on exactly as it is.
2. Add `test/policy.test.js`, driving `src/controller.js`, for what each object
   does under the configuration you are proposing. Exercise what you propose,
   not only what is there today. Leave `src/controller.js` and
   `test/controller.test.js` unchanged and passing; `npm test` must be green.
3. Write `docs/scheduling-review.md`. Answer the draft point by point: for each
   of its three proposals, whether it should apply to each workload, and why.
   Then, per workload: what should happen when a scheduled run is missed, what
   should happen when a run is still going when the next one is due, which field
   on the object implements each decision, and the value you set.
4. In the same document, say what would have made the September miss visible
   inside a day rather than in nine, given what the cluster already alerts on.

each job starts is `src/cron.js`, and it has its own test file.

Rita in Finance opened this on Tuesday. No dunning email has gone to an overdue

dunning run did not happen. That is the part I want you to sit with before you

## Problem Description

1. Add `test/overlap.test.js` for the cases you decide the job has to survive
   before it goes back on. It must run under `node --test` without waiting on
   real elapsed time.
2. If `src/lock.js` or `src/sync.js` need to change, change them.
   `test/lock.test.js` must keep passing unmodified, including the crashed-run
   case.
3. Write `docs/lock-policy.md`: whether the job is safe to switch back on, what
   you changed and why, any staleness value you land on and the measurement it
   comes from, and what now happens to a run that is killed mid-flight.
4. `npm test` must be green when you are done.

assertions: test/overlap.test.js exists and docs/lock-policy.md exists and answers the Monday question one way or the other. A document that describes the lock without giving a verdict on switching the job back on scores at most half.

The answer establishes that no single mtime threshold can satisfy both incidents - the job's own log has runs of 27 and 38 minutes against a ten-minute cycle, so a threshold short enough to return to service by the next invocation steals the lock of a run that is still working, and one above the 41m08s maximum stalls four cycles after a crash - and changes what the age is measured on: the lock is refreshed while the run is alive so that age means idle rather than elapsed, or acquisition turns on whether the recorded holder still exists rather than on the mtime, or the guard becomes an advisory lock the operating system drops when the holding process dies. Delivering a different fixed threshold with no refresh, no holder check and no kernel-held lock scores zero for this criterion however well the number is justified. Full marks require both directions pinned by executed tests that fail against the code as shipped: a lock whose holder is still working, deliberately aged past the threshold, is refused; a lock whose holder is gone is taken by the next invocation. Only one direction tested scores at most half.

MUST NOT recommend re-enabling the sync while the same crontab line is deployed to both hosts in the warehouse group and mutual exclusion rests on a file under /var/run, which ops/fleet.md records as tmpfs on each host with nothing mounted between them. Saying yes to Monday on that arrangement scores zero. Full marks require the July overlap to be read as two hosts rather than two processes on one - the writers in INC-2208 came from 10.4.2.12 and 10.4.2.15, which the host table maps to wh-worker-02 and wh-worker-05, and the role that writes the crontab was applied to the group on 2026-06-02 - and require a stated condition for switching on: the schedule restricted to a single host in a way the role will not undo, or the mutual exclusion moved to the one thing both hosts share, the warehouse database. Treating the file lock as sufficient because its tests pass scores zero; noticing the second host without connecting it to the incident or to the lock path scores at most half.

MUST NOT remove the staleness recovery, set the threshold to Infinity, or make recovery depend on somebody deleting the file by hand. Any of those scores zero: that is INC-1996, four days of a job doing nothing while nobody noticed. test/lock.test.js must pass unmodified, including the case that ages a lock by 25 hours. Full marks additionally require docs/lock-policy.md to say what now happens to a run that is killed mid-flight and how long the schedule waits before it recovers on its own.

docs/lock-policy.md says why the six shipped tests prove less than they appear to: the refusal case measures a lock that is zero milliseconds old, so it passes at any threshold; the recovery case ages a lock by 25 hours, so it also passes at any threshold below a day, including the 60 seconds that was shipped; and no test looks at the lock file after runSync has returned. Citing the green suite as evidence that the lock works scores zero. Noting the tests are thin without saying what makes each of them unable to fail scores at most half.

The answer identifies that runSync releases the lock on the path where it did not acquire it - the finally covers the early return - so an invocation that correctly skips deletes the holder's lock, fixes it so that only the owner releases, and pins it with an executed test showing that after a refused runSync the lock file is still there and a further acquire is still refused. Prose with no test that inspects the lock after a refused runSync scores at most half; not finding it scores zero for this criterion.

The new tests reach their staleness boundaries by setting the lock's timestamps, not by waiting: a suite that sleeps for real seconds or minutes to cross a threshold scores zero, and so does one that only repeats the acquire / release / re-acquire sequence already in test/lock.test.js.
npm test passes on the delivered tree with test/lock.test.js unmodified. A failing suite scores zero, and so does one that reaches green by editing, deleting or skipping an existing test.

# The worker replays what it missed and Ops wants that window widened to thirty days

## Problem Description

We moved the last five scheduled jobs off the old Java service onto the Node
worker. Dmitri did the port in July as a contractor, the Java service was

records the interval each trigger fired on and nothing else. The port replaced
whatever each trigger did about a missed run with one setting for all five: the
window in `src/catchup.js`, which the worker uses at boot to replay what it
missed while it was down.

Last week we found out what that means. A bad deploy took the worker down from
the evening of the 8th to the morning of the 11th. It came back up and replayed
what it had missed inside the window, which is twenty-four hours. Tax reconciled
with the filing partner on Friday: the partner holds no VAT file for the 8th and
none for the 9th. Both were refiled by hand and there is a late-filing penalty
being argued about now.

Sandra has a PR open that raises the window from twenty-four hours to thirty
days so that nothing is ever lost again, and she has asked me to merge it before
Thursday's deploy. On the face of it that is the same fix Tax is asking for.

actually does to each of these five jobs - the job bodies are in
`src/handlers.js` and the adapters they call are in `src/io.js` - because some of

   to a run the worker missed, what you set for it and why, and a direct answer
